hook: A sampler of early FBI flying disc investigation memos from 1947–1949, covering police officer eyewitness reports in Portland, a commercial pilot near-miss in Alaska, the Air Force's retention of civilian photographs taken in Phoenix, and the Bureau's debunking of a Walter Winchell tip about a supposed extraterrestrial landing.
why_it_matters: This section demonstrates that the FBI was functioning as a primary field collection arm for UAP reports in the months immediately following the 1947 wave, coordinating directly with Air Force OSI to share evidence — including physical photographs confiscated from civilian William Rhodes that Rhodes subsequently demanded back. The inter-agency friction over the Rhodes photographs is an early documented instance of the Air Force controlling UAP physical evidence while withholding it from both the original witness and, implicitly, from public view. The multi-witness Portland account is notable for its internal contradictions: a police officer concluded 'ordinary airplane,' while his partner estimated a speed 'much greater than a conventional airplane' and an egg-shape change during flight.

key_findings.finding: Multiple Portland police officers, including the Chief of Police, reported a fast-moving silvery object on September 11, 1947 that changed apparent shape from round to egg-shaped as it turned, with witnesses disagreeing sharply on speed and explanation.

quotes.text: the very bright reflection of the sun on some object which was apparently made of silvery metal. The object was coming from the east and mace a wide turn over the city and disappeared to the south.

JENKINS observed what appeared to be a round silver object, about 10,000 feet high, travelling northeast to southwest...Further observation convinced him that it could not be a balloon because of its speed which was extremely great. As JENKINS watched, it turned gradually until it was travelling due south, and as it did so, its shape seemed to change until it appeared to be egg-shaped. It disappeared in about 30 seconds.
It appeared to him to be elliptical in shape, and inasmuch as it did not bank or tip he could not judge its thickness.

key_findings.finding: A commercial DC-3 pilot and co-pilot near Bethel, Alaska in July 1947 reported a 'flying wing' object with no propeller, no jet exhaust, and no vapor trails, estimated at 300 mph at 1,000 feet; they executed a 45-degree evasive turn and confirmed no aircraft were in the area via radio.

quotes.text: He described the object as appearing to be some flying wing and said that it appeared to be about the size of a 0-54 without any fuselage, He could not see any propellor or any exhaust from jet propulsion or any vapor trails and could not estimate the size due to his failure to be able to estimate the distance he was away from the object.
They made a forty-five degree turn in order to get out of the way of the object and then noted that it appeared to be going away from them.
He called on his radio to the Civil Aeronautics Administration station at Bethel, asking what aircraft was in the vicinity and they had no reports of any aircraft.

key_findings.finding: The Air Force retained photographs of an unidentified object taken by Phoenix civilian William Rhodes, and when Rhodes later requested their return, Air Force OSI coordinated with the FBI Phoenix field office to manage the evidentiary record — while the original Air Force interviewer claimed his recollection of the event was 'hazy.'

quotes.text: concerning his observation and photographing of an object which was considered by the Air Force of significance from a security standpoint.
Mr. Rhodes has apparently now requested the Air Force to return the photographs, which were previously obtained from him.
FUGATE, when questioned by his superiors concerning the matter, stated his recollection was "hazy" on the matter.

key_findings.finding: FBI leadership investigated a Walter Winchell tip about a letter claiming a flying saucer had landed and departed in Los Angeles, theorized to be an extraterrestrial event; investigation found the letter's author, 'Peter Camerlon Jones,' did not exist at the address given.

quotes.text: a letter which Walter Winchell had received from an individual in Los Angeles indicaging that he had seen a flying saucer leave the ground within his view and in which letter he theorized that this might have been a landing, from another planet.

The Los Angeles Office has now advised that the present owner and former manager at this address have no knowledge of any Peter Camerlonxdones and that other investigation to locate Jones was unproductive. It would appear, therefore, that this may have been a prank.

key_findings.finding: Air Force OSI actively sought FBI field office cooperation to compile detailed blind memoranda about UAP witness interviews, revealing a coordinated inter-agency effort to centralize UAP evidence under Air Force control as early as 1949.

quotes.text: Mr. Lynn C. Aldrich, OSI representative at Phoenix, Arizona, has requested the Phoenix Office to furnish him complete facts relating to this interview, which are to be subsequently forwarded to the OSI Office at San Francisco.

Mr. ALDRICH was furnished the substance of the interview...and he has now requested that he be furnished with a blind memorandum setting forth this information in detail in order that he may make it available to the OSI at San Francisco.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: Wright Field and Wright-Patterson are listed among entities in the broader case file, and the Air Force intelligence coordination on the Rhodes photographs originates from Hamilton Field with OSI forwarding to San Francisco, consistent with Wright-Patterson's role as the central repository for UAP physical evidence in this period.

Project Grudge is listed among entities, and these 1947–1949 FBI field reports represent the raw investigative material that directly fed into the predecessor programs to Project Blue Book, including multi-witness police cases and pilot encounters.

The FBI-OSI coordination pipeline for UAP evidence, including the request for 'blind memoranda,' reflects the intelligence community infrastructure that the CIA's later UAP collection efforts would build upon.
